The Six-Month Rule

A T2 is due six months after the day the tax year ends. That is the whole rule, and every other date on this page is produced by applying it to a particular year-end and then adjusting for the calendar.

Fiscal year-endSix months laterT2 due
December 31June 30June 30
March 31September 30September 30
June 30December 31December 31
August 31February 28 or 29The last day of February

The six months are counted to the same day number in the later month. Where that day does not exist, the deadline is the last day of that month, which is why an August 31 year-end lands on the end of February rather than on a non-existent February 31.

Finding Your Fiscal Year-End

A corporation chooses its first fiscal year-end by filing its first T2 with that date on it. Once filed, the year-end is fixed and changing it needs the written approval of the Canada Revenue Agency.

The year-end is not the incorporation anniversary and it is not December 31 by default. If no return has ever been filed, the year-end is still unsettled, and the first return to be filed sets it.

A corporation that has never filed can still choose. A corporation that has filed once cannot, and a return carrying a different year-end from the one on record is the single most common reason a transmission is rejected.

See how to fix a return filed with the wrong year-end.

When the Due Date Falls on a Weekend or Holiday

Where the calculated due date is a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday, the return is on time if the Agency receives it on the next business day.

The holidays that matter are the ones observed where the return is filed, and a provincial holiday can move a date for a corporation in that province while leaving it unmoved elsewhere.

Calculated due dateWhy it movesReturn due
SaturdayNot a business dayThe following Monday
SundayNot a business dayThe following Monday
A statutory holidayNot a business dayThe next business day
A holiday followed by a weekendThree days in a rowThe first business day after all three

The shift can be more than one day. A due date landing on a Sunday followed by a Monday holiday moves to the Tuesday.

The First Tax Year and the 53-Week Limit

A first tax year runs from the date of incorporation to the chosen year-end, and it may not exceed 53 weeks. That is 371 days, counting the day of incorporation.

A year-end chosen more than 53 weeks after incorporation is not available, and the first year has to end earlier, which produces a short first year and then a full one.

See when the first T2 is due after incorporating and the guide to first-year T2 filing.

Short Tax Years and Their Deadlines

A short tax year is any year shorter than twelve months. It arises on a first year, on an approved change of year-end, on an amalgamation and on a final year ending at dissolution.

A short year does not get a short deadline. The six-month rule applies to the day the short year ends, so a three-month year still has six months after it to file.

Short year arises fromYear ends onDeadline measured from
IncorporationThe chosen first year-endThat year-end
An approved year-end changeThe new year-endThat year-end
An amalgamationThe day before amalgamatingThat day
DissolutionThe date of dissolutionThat date

Two returns can therefore be due within a few months of each other, and both are separate filings at $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

The Final Return After Dissolution

A final T2 covers the period from the start of the last tax year to the date of dissolution, and it is due six months after that date.

Every earlier year has to be filed before a corporation can be wound up, so the final return is the last of a sequence rather than a substitute for it.

The sequence is set out in the guide to the final T2 and dissolution.

The Payment Deadline Is Not the Filing Deadline

Filing is due at six months. A balance of tax is due earlier: two months after the year-end, or three months for a Canadian-controlled private corporation that meets the conditions.

ObligationDueOn a nil year
Filing the T2Six months after year-endStill due
Paying the balanceTwo or three months after year-endNothing to pay
InstalmentsMonthly or quarterly through the yearNot required

A corporation with no activity has no balance and no instalments, which leaves the filing deadline as the only one it has to meet.

A Nil Return Has the Same Deadline

There is no separate deadline for a corporation with no activity. The six-month rule applies in full, every year, until the corporation is formally dissolved.

Dormancy is not an exemption and it is not a deferral. A corporation that has done nothing for nine years owes nine returns, each on its own six-month deadline, all of which have passed.

See whether an inactive corporation files every year.

What Happens After the Deadline Passes

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. The unfiled year still stays open forever, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, blocks a clearance certificate and dissolution, and costs a non-resident-owned corporation $25.00 per day up to $2,500.00.

The deadline does not stop mattering once it has gone. It is the date from which the year counts as outstanding, and that is what a demand to file, an arbitrary assessment and a blocked dissolution all follow from.

The full picture is in the guide to T2 late filing penalties.

Provincial Deadlines That Run Separately

Three filings are commonly mistaken for part of the T2 and are not. Each has its own form, its own deadline and its own filing channel.

FilingApplies toRelationship to the T2
Alberta AT1Alberta corporationsA separate return
Quebec CO-17Quebec corporationsA separate return
The annual returnCorporations in most registriesA registry filing, not a tax return

An Alberta corporation files the AT1 as well as the T2, and a Quebec corporation files the CO-17 as well as the T2. Neither is covered by the federal filing and neither is covered by the fee on this page.

See the guide to provincial and federal annual returns.

Working Out Every Deadline You Owe

Start from the year-end on record, add a year at a time up to the present, and apply the six-month rule to each. Every year whose six months have elapsed and which has not been filed is outstanding.

Frequently Asked Questions

When Is a T2 Due?

Six months after the day the tax year ends. A December 31 year-end makes the T2 due June 30, and a March 31 year-end makes it due September 30.

Does a Nil T2 Have a Later Deadline?

No. The six-month rule applies in full to a corporation with no activity, every year, until the corporation is formally dissolved.

What if the Deadline Is a Saturday?

The return is on time if the Canada Revenue Agency receives it on the next business day. The same applies to a Sunday and to a public holiday, and the shift can be more than one day.

How Long Can a First Tax Year Be?

Up to 53 weeks, which is 371 days counting the day of incorporation. A year-end chosen beyond that is not available.

Is the Payment Deadline the Same as the Filing Deadline?

No. Filing is due at six months, while a balance of tax is due two months after the year-end, or three for a Canadian-controlled private corporation that meets the conditions. A nil year has no balance to pay.

Does a Short Tax Year Get a Shorter Deadline?

No. The six-month rule is measured from the day the short year ends, so a three-month year still has six months after it to file.

What Zero Activity Means on a Return

Zero activity means the corporation had no revenue, no expenses, no income of any kind and no disposition of property during the tax year. The return is filed showing those amounts as $0.00.

It is a statement about the tax year, not about the corporation. The same corporation can have a zero-activity year, then a trading year, then another zero-activity year, and each is assessed on its own.

Zero activity is a property of the twelve months, which is why the question is always asked year by year and never once for the life of the corporation.

Why a Zero-Activity Corporation Still Files

Every resident corporation files a T2 for every tax year, whether or not it did anything. The obligation attaches to existing as a corporation, not to earning income.

The return is how the Agency learns the year was zero. Without it the year is not recorded as zero, it is recorded as missing.

See whether a corporation with no activity files.

The Tests That Decide Whether a Year Is Nil

Six questions settle it. A single yes takes the year out of zero activity, and the questions are asked about the tax year rather than about today.

QuestionIf yes
Was there any revenue?Not a zero-activity year
Were there any expenses?Not a zero-activity year
Was there investment income of any amount?Not a zero-activity year
Was there rental income?Not a zero-activity year
Was a dividend paid or received?Not a zero-activity year
Was any property disposed of?Not a zero-activity year

Amount is irrelevant to every row. Four dollars of interest answers the third question yes exactly as four thousand would.

What Looks Like Zero Activity and Is Not

These are the entries that most often turn up on a year the directors believed was empty.

EntryWhy it is not zero activity
Bank interest credited to a corporate accountInvestment income, whatever the amount
An annual registry fee paid from the corporate accountAn expense
Accounting or filing fees paid by the corporationAn expense
Rent received on a property the corporation ownsRental income
A dividend received from another corporationIncome, and it changes the schedules
Sale of equipment the corporation still heldA disposition

A holding corporation with investment income, a rental corporation and a corporation that paid or received a dividend are not nil. Those are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

A shareholder paying the registry fee personally, from a personal account, and not charging it to the corporation, leaves the year zero.

No Bank Account and No Business Number

Neither changes the filing obligation. A corporation with no bank account files, and a corporation that was never given a business number files once it has one.

A corporation with no bank account has one advantage on this page: with no account there is no credited interest, so the most common accidental entry cannot arise.

See filing with no bank account and whether a business number is needed.

Which Schedules a Zero-Activity Return Carries

A zero-activity return is not an empty return. Several schedules are filed carrying zeroes, and one of them is filed only once.

ScheduleOn a zero-activity year
Schedule 100, the balance sheetFiled, carrying the balances
Schedule 125, the income statementFiled, carrying zeroes
Schedule 141, the notes checklistFiled
Schedule 24On a first return only
Schedule 50For every shareholder at 10% or more
Schedule 8Filed where the corporation holds depreciable property

The full set is in the guide to T2 schedules on a nil return.

Reporting Zeroes Through the GIFI

The General Index of Financial Information is the coded format the balance sheet and income statement are filed in. A zero-activity year reports through it the same way a trading year does, with zeroes in the income statement codes.

The balance sheet is rarely all zeroes. Share capital issued on incorporation, a shareholder loan and retained earnings carried forward all sit on Schedule 100 whether or not anything happened during the year.

A balance sheet filed as entirely zero when share capital was issued is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that persists: the next return opens from the closing balances this one reports.

See the guide to GIFI Schedules 100, 125 and 141.

The T2 Short on a Zero-Activity Year

The T2 Short is a two-page version of the return available to a Canadian-controlled private corporation that meets a list of conditions. A zero-activity year commonly meets them.

Meeting the conditions is not automatic. A second permanent establishment, a reporting currency other than the Canadian dollar, a refundable credit or an amalgamation in the year each rule it out.

Eligibility is set out in the guide to T2 Short eligibility.

Several Zero-Activity Years at Once

Each year is its own return on its own form for its own tax year. Six zero-activity years are six returns, and they are prepared oldest first so the closing balances of one open the next.

They can be prepared and transmitted together. Each is $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

See filing five years at once and the guide to catching up on unfiled corporate tax returns.

Leaving a Zero-Activity Year Unfiled

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. The unfiled year still stays open forever, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, blocks a clearance certificate and dissolution, and costs a non-resident-owned corporation $25.00 per day up to $2,500.00.

The year with nothing in it is the one most often left, and it is the one that blocks a dissolution years later. A corporation cannot be wound up with an open year on its record, however empty that year was.

When Activity Starts

The year activity begins is not a zero-activity year, even if it begins in the last week of it. Revenue in December makes the whole year a trading year.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Counts as Zero Activity?

No revenue, no expenses, no income of any kind and no disposition of property during the tax year. The return is filed showing those amounts as $0.00.

Does Bank Interest Take a Year Out of Zero Activity?

Yes. Interest credited to a corporate account is investment income whatever the amount, and a few dollars answers the question the same way a few thousand would.

Is a Zero-Activity Return an Empty Return?

No. The income statement carries zeroes, but the balance sheet carries share capital, any shareholder loan and retained earnings brought forward, and Schedule 50 still reports every shareholder at 10% or more.

Does a Corporation With No Bank Account Still File?

Yes. The obligation attaches to existing as a corporation. With no account there is no credited interest, so the year is more likely to be genuinely zero.

Yes. They are six separate returns prepared oldest first, so the closing balances of each open the next, and they can be transmitted in one sitting at $300.00 plus HST per tax year each.

What if Activity Started Late in the Year?

Arrears Guide

The Complete Guide to Corporate Tax Arrears and Interest

What Corporate Tax Arrears Are

Arrears are an unpaid balance on a corporation's tax account. The balance can come from an assessed return, from a reassessment, from an assessment the Agency raised on its own estimate, or from a charge added to the account.

Arrears are a balance, not a filing. A corporation can be years behind on filing and owe nothing, and it can be fully filed and owe a great deal.

Separating the two is the point of this page. The rest of it is about which one a dormant corporation actually has.

How Interest Is Charged on an Unpaid Balance

Interest runs on an unpaid balance and compounds daily. It starts from the day the balance was due and continues until the balance is paid.

It attaches to the balance, which means it needs a balance to attach to. Interest is not charged on a return that was filed late and showed nothing owing.

ChargeAttaches toNeeds
InterestAn unpaid balanceA balance owing
Instalment interestInstalments not paid when dueAn instalment obligation
Percentage late-filing penaltyTax owing on the returnTax owing

All three columns describe the same dependency from different sides. None of the three has anything to work on where the corporation owes $0.00.

Why a Nil Year Produces No Arrears

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. The unfiled year still stays open forever, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, blocks a clearance certificate and dissolution, and costs a non-resident-owned corporation $25.00 per day up to $2,500.00.

A year with no activity assesses at $0.00. There is no balance, so there is nothing for interest to compound on and nothing for the percentage charge to be a percentage of.

That is the end of the matter only while the year is filed. The next section is about what happens when it is not.

Arbitrary Assessments and Manufactured Arrears

Where a return is not filed and a demand to file goes unanswered, the Agency may assess the corporation on its own estimate of income. The amount is an estimate the corporation did not supply.

That assessment creates a real balance. Interest then runs on it, and the corporation is in arrears on a figure it never earned.

This is how a dormant corporation that genuinely owed nothing ends up with a collectible debt and interest compounding daily. The balance was not produced by activity. It was produced by the missing return.

An arbitrary assessment stands until a filed return displaces it, which makes filing the only way to remove it. See what happens if a demand to file goes unanswered.

Instalment Interest

A corporation with tax owing above the threshold pays by instalments through the year. Where an instalment is missed or paid short, interest is charged on the shortfall.

A corporation with no activity has no instalment obligation, so it cannot incur instalment interest. The obligation arises from the previous year's tax, and a nil year sets that at $0.00.

YearTax owingInstalments the following year
A nil year$0.00None required
A trading year below the thresholdSmallNone required
A trading year above the thresholdAbove the thresholdMonthly or quarterly

A corporation emerging from dormancy into a profitable year is the case to watch, because its instalment position for the following year changes.

The Order Payments Are Applied In

A payment to a tax account is not applied to whichever year the payer had in mind. It is applied according to the Agency's own ordering, and interest already accrued is generally taken before the balance it accrued on.

The practical consequence is that a partial payment reduces a balance more slowly than the payer expects, because part of it clears interest that then stops growing only from that date.

None of this reaches a corporation whose years are all nil. It matters to a corporation that traded, stopped, and left a balance behind.

Taxpayer Relief and What It Covers

The Agency may cancel or waive interest and penalties in defined circumstances. Relief is discretionary, it is requested in writing, and it is decided on the facts of the particular account.

Relief can be requested forRelief does not extend to
Interest charged on a balanceThe underlying tax itself
A late-filing penaltyThe obligation to file the return
Charges arising from circumstances beyond the corporation's controlA decision not to file

Relief is not a route around filing. The return still has to be filed, and a request made while years remain outstanding has little to work with.

Collections and Director Liability

An assessed balance is collectible. The Agency has statutory collection powers it can use without going to court, and it can act on a balance produced by an arbitrary assessment exactly as on one produced by a filed return.

Certain amounts a corporation was required to withhold and remit, including payroll source deductions and net GST/HST, can be assessed against directors personally. Corporate income tax on its own is not among them.

A dormant corporation with an unclosed payroll or GST/HST account is the case where this becomes personal. Closing those accounts is covered in the guide to winding up an inactive corporation.

Clearing Arrears Created by an Unfiled Year

Filing the actual return is what removes an arbitrary assessment. The filed figures displace the estimate, and a nil year reassesses to $0.00.

Interest that accrued on the estimated balance falls away with the balance it was charged on. Where charges remain after reassessment, that is when a relief request has something definite to address.

StepEffect
File the outstanding yearDisplaces the estimate
The year reassesses at $0.00The balance goes
Interest charged on that balanceFalls away with it
Anything left standingCan be put to a relief request

Oldest year first, each on its own return. See how to catch up on years of unfiled returns.

How Long Arrears Last

A collectible balance does not expire on a fixed anniversary. Collection limitation periods can be restarted by Agency action and by acknowledgement of the debt, so a balance left alone is not a balance running down.

An unfiled year does not expire at all. There is no point at which it closes itself, which is why an arbitrary assessment raised years ago can still be sitting on an account today.

Keeping a Dormant Corporation Out of Arrears

A dormant corporation stays out of arrears by filing each year on time. That is the whole mechanism: with the year filed at $0.00 there is no estimate, no balance and nothing to compound.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a Nil Year Create Arrears?

No. A year with no activity assesses at $0.00, so there is no balance for interest to compound on and nothing for a percentage charge to apply to.

How Can a Dormant Corporation Owe Money Then?

Through an arbitrary assessment. Where a return is unfiled and a demand goes unanswered, the Canada Revenue Agency may assess on its own estimate of income, and interest then runs on that estimated balance.

Does Filing the Return Remove an Arbitrary Assessment?

Yes. The filed figures displace the estimate, a nil year reassesses to $0.00, and interest charged on the estimated balance falls away with it.

Does Interest Run on a Return Filed Late With Nothing Owing?

No. Interest attaches to an unpaid balance, so it needs a balance to attach to.

Can Directors Be Held Personally Liable?

For amounts the corporation was required to withhold and remit, including payroll source deductions and net GST/HST, yes. Corporate income tax on its own is not among them.

Do Arrears Expire if Left Alone?

A collection limitation period can be restarted by Agency action and by acknowledgement of the debt, so a balance left alone is not a balance running down. An unfiled year does not expire at all.

Winding Up Is Two Separate Processes

Closing a corporation involves two authorities that do not talk to each other on your behalf. The tax side is settled with the Canada Revenue Agency. The legal existence of the corporation is ended by the registry it was incorporated under.

SideWhoWhat it ends
TaxCanada Revenue AgencyThe filing and remittance obligations
LegalThe incorporating registryThe corporation's existence

Doing one and not the other is the usual failure. A corporation struck from a registry with open tax years still has those years open, and a corporation fully filed but never dissolved keeps acquiring new filing obligations every year.

The Order the Steps Have to Happen In

The sequence is not a preference. Each step depends on the one before it, and taking them out of order is what leaves a wind-up half-finished for years.

OrderStepDepends on
1File every outstanding tax yearNothing
2Distribute or dispose of the remaining assetsKnowing the tax position
3Request a clearance certificateStep 1 being complete
4File articles of dissolution with the registryStep 3
5File the final T2The date of dissolution existing
6Close the remaining accountsStep 5

Step 5 comes after step 4 because the final return runs to the date of dissolution, and that date does not exist until the registry sets it.

Every Return Due Before You Can Wind Up

A corporation cannot be wound up cleanly with an open year on its record. Every tax year from incorporation to the present has to be filed, including the years in which nothing happened.

Nine dormant years are nine returns. They are prepared oldest first and can be transmitted together, each at $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

This is the step that stops most wind-ups. The directors discover the open years at the point of requesting a clearance certificate, which is the latest possible moment to find out.

See whether a corporation can be dissolved with unfiled returns.

The Clearance Certificate

A clearance certificate is the Agency's confirmation that the corporation has no outstanding amounts. It protects the directors personally: distributing the corporation's property without one can leave them liable for amounts the corporation turns out to owe.

It is requested in writing and it cannot be issued while a year is unfiled.

Clearance certificatePosition
All years filed, nothing owingCan be issued
A year unfiledCannot be issued
A balance outstandingNot until the balance is settled
Assets already distributed without oneDirectors exposed to the corporation's liabilities

A dormant corporation with all years filed at $0.00 is the simplest case there is for a clearance request.

The Final T2

The final return covers the period from the start of the last tax year to the date of dissolution. It is due six months after that date.

It is marked as the final return, which is what tells the Agency to expect no further years. Without that marking the account stays open and the corporation keeps appearing to owe returns.

The return itself is covered in full in the guide to the final T2 and dissolution, and the year of dissolution answers whether that year is still owed.

Closing the GST/HST and Payroll Accounts

A corporation often has program accounts beyond the corporate income tax one. Each is closed separately, and each keeps generating obligations until it is.

AccountClosed byUntil it is closed
GST/HSTForm RC145Nil returns remain due
PayrollForm RC145Nil remittances remain expected
Corporate income taxThe final T2, marked finalT2 returns remain due

An unclosed payroll or GST/HST account is the one that can reach the directors personally, because those are amounts the corporation was required to withhold or collect and remit.

Closing the accounts is not covered by the fee on this page. See closing a corporate tax account after dissolution.

Distributing Assets Before Dissolution

A corporation cannot be dissolved holding property. Whatever it still owns is distributed to the shareholders or disposed of first, and both have tax consequences the final return reports.

A disposition is activity. A corporation that sells or transfers property in its last period does not have a nil final year, and that return is handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

A genuinely empty corporation, holding nothing but perhaps a nominal share balance, has nothing to distribute and a nil final year.

Articles of Dissolution

The registry ends the corporation's existence on receiving articles of dissolution, and the date it records is the date the final tax period runs to.

The registry is the one the corporation was incorporated under: the federal registry for a federally incorporated corporation, and the provincial registry otherwise. Filing with the wrong one achieves nothing.

IncorporatedDissolved throughSeparate annual return
FederallyThe federal registryYes, with its own fee
In a provinceThat province's registryDepends on the province

The annual return is a registry filing and not a tax return. See the guide to provincial and federal annual returns.

What Can Still Arrive After Dissolution

Dissolution does not seal the record. An assessment, a reassessment or a demand relating to a period before dissolution can still be issued, and a return for a pre-dissolution year can still be filed.

Keeping the clearance certificate and the dissolution record is what makes those straightforward to deal with.

See filing a T2 after dissolution and returns left unfiled after dissolution.

Revival and Involuntary Dissolution

A corporation struck by a registry for failing to file its annual return has not been wound up. It has been dissolved involuntarily, with its tax years still open and nothing settled.

Registries provide for revival, which restores the corporation so the outstanding filings can be made and a proper wind-up completed. The open tax years survived the striking and are waiting.

A corporation found in this state is usually in it because the annual return lapsed, not because anyone decided to close it. The tax years are the part nobody looked at.

See dissolving a corporation that never filed.

Keeping the Records Afterwards

Corporate records are kept after dissolution, not discarded with it. The books, the returns, the clearance certificate and the dissolution record all remain relevant for years.

Form T183CORP for each year filed here is retained for six years and is never backdated. The signing record is covered in the guide to Form T183CORP signing and transmission.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I Dissolve a Corporation With Unfiled T2 Returns?

Not cleanly. A clearance certificate cannot be issued while a year is unfiled, and distributing the corporation's property without one can leave the directors personally liable.

What Order Do the Steps Go In?

File every outstanding year, deal with the remaining assets, request a clearance certificate, file articles of dissolution, then file the final T2 and close the remaining accounts. The final return runs to the dissolution date, so it comes after the registry sets that date.

Is a Clearance Certificate Compulsory?

It is not a filing requirement, but distributing the corporation's property without one exposes the directors to amounts the corporation turns out to owe. For a dormant corporation with every year filed at $0.00 it is the simplest case there is.

Do I Have to Close the GST/HST and Payroll Accounts Separately?

Yes. Each is closed with Form RC145, and until it is closed nil returns and nil remittances remain due on it. Those closures are not covered by the fee for a nil T2.

What if the Registry Already Struck the Corporation?

It was dissolved involuntarily and its tax years are still open. Registries provide for revival, which restores the corporation so the outstanding filings can be made and a proper wind-up completed.

Does Dissolution Close the Tax Record?

No. An assessment, a reassessment or a demand relating to a pre-dissolution period can still be issued, and a return for such a year can still be filed.

Deciding Whether Your Year Is Nil

The return is nil where the corporation had no revenue, no expenses, no income of any kind and no disposition of property in the tax year. Amount does not come into it.

A holding corporation with investment income, a rental corporation and a corporation that paid or received a dividend are not nil. Those are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

The Annual Return Is a Separate Filing

The annual return is filed with the registry the corporation was incorporated under. It confirms the directors, the registered office and the corporation's continued existence. It reports no income and it is not a tax return.

What Belongs on a Corporate Compliance Calendar

A compliance calendar holds the dates a corporation owes something to somebody, whether or not it traded. Two kinds of date sit on it, and they behave differently.

Kind of dateDerived fromExample
Year-end drivenThe corporation's own fiscal year-endThe T2 deadline
Anniversary drivenThe date of incorporationThe annual return in some registries
Fixed calendarThe calendar yearThe T4 deadline at the end of February

No two corporations have the same calendar unless they share a year-end and an incorporation date, which is why a calendar has to be derived rather than copied.

The T2 Deadline

Six months after the fiscal year-end, every year, for every corporation. This is the one date on the calendar that never has an exception.

A balance of tax, where there is one, is due earlier: two months after the year-end, or three for a Canadian-controlled private corporation meeting the conditions. A corporation with no activity has no balance.

Every year-end and its due date is listed on the deadlines page, and the rules behind them are in the guide to T2 filing deadlines.

The Annual Return Deadline

The annual return is a registry filing. It confirms the directors, the registered office and that the corporation still exists, and it reports no income.

Its date is set by the registry rather than by the tax year, and it is commonly tied to the anniversary of incorporation. A federally incorporated corporation files one with its own fee.

This is the filing whose absence gets a corporation struck from a registry. A corporation can be perfectly current on tax and still be dissolved involuntarily for missing it.

See the guide to provincial and federal annual returns.

Provincial Returns and Their Own Dates

Two provinces collect corporate income tax on their own returns, filed separately from the T2 and on their own deadlines.

ProvinceReturnRelationship to the T2

QuebecCO-17A separate return with its own deadline
ElsewhereNoneProvincial tax is calculated within the T2

GST/HST Filing Dates

A corporation with a GST/HST account files on the frequency assigned to it: monthly, quarterly or annually. The frequency determines the dates, and the account generates them whether or not there was any activity.

A nil GST/HST return is still a return. It does not disappear because there was nothing to report, and it is not covered by the fee for a nil T2.

The account is closed with Form RC145, which is the only thing that stops the dates recurring.

Payroll Remittance and the T4

A payroll account carries two kinds of date: the remittance dates through the year and the annual information return.

ObligationTimingWith no employees
Source deduction remittancesOn the assigned frequencyNil remittances expected
T4 information returnThe end of FebruaryStill expected while the account is open

Remittance amounts are the ones that can be assessed against directors personally, which makes an unused open payroll account worth closing rather than ignoring.

Changing a Fiscal Year-End

A year-end is fixed by the first return filed and changing it needs the written approval of the Canada Revenue Agency. The change is not made by filing a return with a different date on it.

An approved change produces a short tax year, and the whole calendar moves with it: the T2 date, the balance date and the instalment pattern all shift.

See fixing a return filed with the wrong year-end.

Registered Office and Director Changes

These are not annual dates. They are event-driven, and the clock starts when the change happens rather than at a year-end.

A registry has to be told within a set period of a change of registered office or of directors. A corporation whose registered address is stale is a corporation that does not receive the registry notice warning it is about to be struck.

A dormant corporation is the most likely to have a stale address, because nobody is checking the post at an office nobody uses.

The Minute Book and Annual Resolutions

The minute book holds the articles, the register of directors and shareholders, the share certificates and the resolutions. It is maintained whether or not the corporation traded.

Annual resolutions are passed each year even in a dormant corporation: the shareholders consider the year, appoint or reappoint directors, and record the decision. A nil year has a short minute, not no minute.

Shareholdings recorded there are what Schedule 50 reports. See the guide to Schedule 50 and shareholder reporting.

Once the unused accounts are closed, a dormant corporation's calendar reduces to two recurring items and one maintained record.

The nil T2Annually, six months after year-endThe year stays open indefinitely
The annual returnAnnually, per the registryThe corporation can be struck
The minute bookMaintainedGaps in the corporate record

That is the floor. It cannot be reduced further while the corporation exists, and the only way to end it is to wind the corporation up.

See the guide to winding up an inactive corporation.

Building Your Own Calendar From Your Year-End

Take the year-end on record, add six months for the T2, add the registry date for the annual return, and add the frequency dates for any account still open. Everything else is event-driven.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Dates Does a Dormant Corporation Actually Owe?

Once unused accounts are closed, two recurring filings: the nil T2 six months after each fiscal year-end, and the annual return on the registry's date. The minute book is maintained alongside them.

Is the Annual Return on the Same Date as the T2?

Yes. The shareholders still consider the year and record the decision. A nil year has a short minute rather than no minute.

Because that is where a registry sends the notice warning that a corporation is about to be struck for a missed annual return. A dormant corporation is the most likely to have a stale address on file.

Keeping a numbered company current between returns: the registry, the registered office, the minute book and the years nobody filed. Nil T2 filing is $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

What a Numbered Company Is

A numbered company is a corporation that was incorporated without choosing a name, so the registry assigned it a number instead. In Ontario that reads as a seven-digit number followed by Ontario Inc.

The number is the corporation's legal name. It is not a placeholder and it does not need replacing.

Incorporating with a number is a deliberate choice, often because a name search was not wanted or the corporation was set up to hold something rather than to trade under a brand.

A Number Changes Nothing About Filing

Every obligation a named corporation has, a numbered one has identically. The return, the schedules, the deadlines and the annual return are the same.

ObligationNamed corporationNumbered corporation
Annual T2YesYes
Nil return when inactiveYesYes
Six-month deadlineYesYes
Annual return with the registryYesYes
Dissolution to end the obligationsYesYes

The guide to numbered company tax filing covers the return itself.

Finding Your Corporation Number and Business Number

Two different numbers are in play, issued by two different bodies, and they are routinely confused.

NumberIssued byUsed for
Corporation numberThe incorporating registryRegistry filings and the corporation's identity
Business numberThe Canada Revenue AgencyTax accounts, including the T2

A corporation can have a corporation number and no business number if it never registered for anything. The business number is obtained before the first return is transmitted.

See whether a business number is needed to file.

The Annual Return and the Registry

The annual return keeps the corporation on the register. It confirms the directors, the registered office and that the corporation still exists, and it reports no income.

A numbered company is the most common casualty of a missed annual return, because there is no trading activity reminding anyone it exists.

Missing it does not produce a charge. It produces a striking: the registry dissolves the corporation involuntarily, while its tax years stay open and unsettled.

See the guide to provincial and federal annual returns.

Keeping the Registered Office Current

The registered office is the address the registry and the Agency write to. A change has to be filed within the period the registry sets.

A numbered holding company whose registered office is a former accountant's address, or a home the shareholder moved out of, receives nothing. The warning that it is about to be struck goes to an address nobody reads.

This is the least demanding piece of maintenance there is, and the one most often left.

Director Records

Directors are recorded with the registry and changes are filed when they happen. A corporation whose sole director has died or resigned without a replacement is not properly constituted.

Directors remain exposed to certain corporate amounts, including payroll source deductions and net GST/HST, which makes an accurate record a matter of personal interest rather than paperwork.

EventFiled with the registryTiming
A director appointedYesWithin the registry's period
A director resignedYesWithin the registry's period
A director's address changedYesWithin the registry's period

None of these are tax filings and none are covered by the fee on this page.

The Minute Book

The minute book holds the articles, the registers of directors and shareholders, the share certificates and the resolutions. It is the corporation's own record of itself.

It is maintained through dormant years. Annual resolutions are still passed, and the shareholdings recorded in it are what Schedule 50 reports on the return.

See the guide to Schedule 50 and shareholder reporting.

Nil Years on a Numbered Company

A numbered company that holds nothing and does nothing files a nil T2 for every tax year, six months after each year-end, until it is dissolved.

A holding corporation with investment income, a rental corporation and a corporation that paid or received a dividend are not nil. Those are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

Each year is $300.00 plus HST per tax year. See what happens when a numbered company does not file.

The Forgotten Numbered Company

A numbered company set up years ago for a purpose that never materialised is the commonest version of this. Nobody traded through it, nobody filed for it, and it has been quietly accruing open years.

Those years can all be filed. They are prepared oldest first and transmitted together, and a corporation nobody used has the simplest possible set of figures.

Finding the corporation number, the year-end on record and the list of open years is the first step, and it is usually the only part that takes any effort.

See filing for a corporation you forgot about and the guide to catching up on unfiled corporate tax returns.

Adding an Operating Name Later

A numbered company can register a business name to trade under without changing its legal name. The number remains the corporation's name on every filing.

Registering a business name is a registry matter and has no effect on the T2. The return continues to be filed in the corporation's numbered name.

Trading under the new name is, of course, trading. That year is not a nil year.

Closing a Numbered Company

Maintenance ends only at dissolution. Until then the corporation exists and acquires a new filing obligation every year, whether or not anyone is attending to it.

Every outstanding year is filed first, then a clearance certificate, then articles of dissolution, then the final T2 running to the dissolution date.

The sequence is in the guide to winding up an inactive corporation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a Numbered Company Treated Differently by the Agency?

No. Every obligation a named corporation has, a numbered one has identically: the return, the schedules, the deadlines and the annual return.

What Is the Difference Between a Corporation Number and a Business Number?

The corporation number is issued by the incorporating registry and is used for registry filings. The business number is issued by the Canada Revenue Agency and is used for tax accounts, including the T2.

What Happens if a Numbered Company Misses Its Annual Return?

The registry can dissolve it involuntarily. That is a striking rather than a charge, and the corporation's tax years stay open and unsettled afterwards.

Does a Numbered Company That Holds Nothing Still File?

Yes, a nil T2 for every tax year, six months after each year-end, until it is formally dissolved.

Can I File for a Numbered Company I Forgot I Had?

Yes. The open years are prepared oldest first and can be transmitted together. A corporation nobody used has the simplest possible set of figures.

Can a Numbered Company Trade Under a Name?

It can register a business name to trade under while its legal name remains the number. Registering the name has no effect on the T2, though trading under it means that year is not nil.

The Rule for Tax Years Starting After 2023

For tax years beginning after 2023, electronic filing of the T2 is mandatory for virtually all corporations. It is not a preference and it is not limited to large corporations.

The change removed a threshold that had previously exempted smaller corporations from mandatory electronic filing. The obligation now reaches almost every corporation that files a T2 at all.

The rule is about the method, not the content. A return with nothing in it is transmitted electronically exactly as a return with everything in it.

Which Corporations It Applies To

Virtually all of them. The exceptions are narrow and defined, and a corporation with no activity is not among them.

CorporationElectronic filing

A numbered company holding nothingMandatory
Filing a first returnMandatory

Every row above is a corporation this site files for, and every one of them is transmitted electronically.

The Paper Filing Penalty

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. The unfiled year still stays open forever, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, blocks a clearance certificate and dissolution, and costs a non-resident-owned corporation $25.00 per day up to $2,500.00.

That block is about filing late. The charge for filing on paper is a different thing entirely, and it is the reason this guide exists: a paper T2 draws a flat $1,000.00, and a flat amount does not care that the corporation owes $0.00.

ChargeCalculated asOn a nil return
Percentage late-filing chargeA percentage of tax owing$0.00, because the tax owing is $0.00
Paper filing chargeA flat amount per return$1,000.00 in full

Read the right-hand column. The two charges behave in opposite ways on the same return.

The Preparer Penalty

A separate charge of $100.00 per return applies to a preparer who files a corporate return on paper where electronic filing was required.

It attaches to the person who prepared and filed the return, not to the corporation. A professional preparer filing on paper is exposed to it on every return.

Returns here are transmitted electronically by a registered EFILE electronic filer, so neither charge arises.

A Nil Return Is Not Exempt

Nothing about having no activity removes the electronic filing obligation or the charge for ignoring it. A dormant corporation that posts a paper T2 is exposed to the full $1,000.00 on a return reporting $0.00.

This is the largest single amount a genuinely nil corporation can be charged, and the only one it can incur by being careful in the wrong way. Posting the return is not the safe option.

See whether a nil T2 can be filed without an accountant.

How an Electronic Return Reaches the Agency

The return is prepared in certified software, validated against the Agency's rules, and transmitted directly. There is no envelope, no posting date and no question about whether it arrived.

Form T183CORP and Electronic Signing

Form T183CORP is what authorises the transmission. It carries the figures from the return it belongs to, and it is signed by an authorized signing officer of the corporation before anything is sent.

It is signed here on a single-use access-controlled screen, with the date and the time recorded. It is never backdated, it is kept for six years, and it is not sent to the Agency unless the Agency asks for it.

The full detail is in the guide to Form T183CORP signing and transmission.

What Happens When a Transmission Is Rejected

A rejected transmission is not a filed return. The Agency returns an error identifying what it would not accept, the return is corrected, and it is sent again.

Common rejectionCause
Year-end does not match the recordA different year-end than the one on file
Business number not recognisedA wrong number, or no account for the return type
A required schedule missingA schedule the return's own answers made mandatory
Balances do not carry forwardOpening figures that do not match the prior year's close

One corrected transmission is included in the fee where the Agency rejects the first one. The year-end mismatch is the most frequent of the four, and fixing a wrong year-end covers it.

The Confirmation You Receive

An accepted transmission produces a confirmation from the Agency. That is the evidence the year was filed, and it is what a clearance request, a dissolution and a lender all eventually ask for.

It is emailed within 3 business days of transmission. Keep it with the corporate records: it is easier to retain than to retrieve years later.

A return nobody can evidence is, in practice, a return that gets filed twice. The confirmation takes no effort to keep and a great deal of effort to reconstruct years later.

The Narrow Exceptions

A small number of corporations fall outside mandatory electronic filing, defined by what the corporation is rather than by how little it did. An insurer, a non-resident corporation in certain circumstances and a corporation reporting in a functional currency are the kinds of case involved.

Being dormant is not an exception, having no bank account is not an exception, and finding the software inconvenient is not an exception.

A holding corporation with investment income, a rental corporation and a corporation that paid or received a dividend are not nil. Those are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

Filing Older Years Electronically

Earlier tax years are transmitted electronically too. Catching up on six unfiled years does not mean posting six paper returns, and the Agency accepts prior-year returns through the same channel.

For tax years beginning after 2023 it is mandatory for virtually all corporations. The earlier threshold that exempted smaller corporations was removed.

A flat $1,000.00, plus a separate $100.00 per-return charge on the preparer. Neither is a percentage of anything.

The Complete Guide to Schedule 50 and Shareholder Reporting

What Schedule 50 reports, the 10% threshold, what goes in each row, and why a nil return still files it in full. Nil T2 filing is $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

What Schedule 50 Reports

Schedule 50 is the shareholder information schedule. It lists the people and entities holding a significant stake in the corporation, and it is filed with the T2.

It reports ownership, not money. No income, no dividend and no valuation appears on it.

It is the schedule that tells the Agency who stands behind the corporation. That is why it survives on a return where every financial figure is $0.00.

The 10% Threshold

A shareholder is reported where they hold 10% or more of any class of shares. Below 10% of every class, they are not reported.

HoldingReported on Schedule 50
Sole shareholder, 100%Yes
Two shareholders at 50% eachBoth
Four shareholders at 25% eachAll four
A shareholder at 10% exactlyYes, the threshold is inclusive
A shareholder at 9%No
9% of common but 40% of preferredYes, on the strength of the preferred class

The last two rows are the ones to read together. The test runs class by class, so a holding that is small in one class and large in another is reported.

What Goes in Each Row

Each reported shareholder takes a row carrying their identifying details and the holding itself.

FieldFor an individualFor a corporation
NameFull legal nameFull legal name
IdentifierSocial insurance numberBusiness number
Share class heldThe classThe class
Percentage heldOf that classOf that class

An identifier that does not match the Agency's record is a frequent cause of a rejected transmission, and it is worth checking before the return is sent rather than after.

Schedule 50 on a Nil Return

It is filed in full. A corporation with no activity still has shareholders, and who they are has not changed because the corporation did nothing.

This is what people mean when they find a nil return is not an empty return. The income statement is zeroes, and Schedule 50 carries real names and real percentages.

The other schedules a nil return carries are in the guide to T2 schedules on a nil return.

One price for every year and every province. CPA reviewed and transmitted electronically.

Corporate and Trust Shareholders

A shareholder does not have to be a person. Where a corporation holds 10% or more, it is reported with its business number rather than a social insurance number.

A holding structure is therefore visible on the schedule: the operating corporation reports its parent, and the parent reports its own shareholders.

A holding corporation receiving a dividend from the corporation below it does not have a nil year. A holding corporation with investment income, a rental corporation and a corporation that paid or received a dividend are not nil. Those are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

See the guide to inactive holding company filing.

Shareholder Changes During the Year

The schedule reflects the holdings as the return reports them for the tax year. A transfer during the year is reflected in what the schedule shows, and the minute book is what evidences it.

A transfer of shares is not by itself income to the corporation, so it does not take a quiet year out of nil. What a transfer changes is the schedule, not the income statement.

Where shares were sold by a shareholder, that is the shareholder's personal matter rather than the corporation's.

The Errors That Get Returns Rejected

Schedule 50 produces a disproportionate share of rejections, because it is the schedule carrying identifiers the Agency can check against its own records.

ErrorResult
A social insurance number that does not match the nameRejected transmission
A business number for a corporate shareholder that is wrongRejected transmission
Percentages for a class totalling more than 100Validation failure
A 10% shareholder omittedAn incomplete return
Reporting by overall ownership instead of class by classShareholders wrongly included or left out

The last row is the conceptual error rather than a typing one, and it is the one that survives a careful proofread.

Related and Associated Corporations

Schedule 50 is not the schedule that reports related or associated corporations. It reports shareholders. Relatedness and association are separate concepts with their own schedules and their own consequences.

Association matters on a trading return because it affects how much of the small business deduction is available. On a nil return there is nothing to allocate, which is why the subject rarely arises here.

A corporation in a group with trading members has figures to report and is handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

Shareholder Loans Are Reported Elsewhere

A balance owed to or by a shareholder is a balance sheet item. It appears on Schedule 100 through the GIFI, not on Schedule 50.

A shareholder loan does not by itself produce income or expense, so a dormant corporation carrying one on its balance sheet can still have a nil year.

ItemReported on
Who the shareholders areSchedule 50

Share capital issuedSchedule 100, the balance sheet
A dividend paid to a shareholderThe return, and it ends the nil year

See the guide to GIFI Schedules 100, 125 and 141.

Dividends Take the Year Out of Nil

A dividend paid or received is activity. The corporation that pays one does not have a nil year, and neither does the corporation that receives one.

Schedule 50 still reports the shareholders in such a year, but the return is no longer a nil return and is not the service this page describes.

The handover is described at when your corporation starts operating.

Who Can See Schedule 50

Schedule 50 is filed with the Agency and is subject to the confidentiality rules that cover a corporation's tax information. It is not a public register and it is not published.

The public record of ownership, where one exists, is the registry's, not the Agency's, and the two hold different information.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Has to Be Reported on Schedule 50?

Any shareholder holding 10% or more of any class of shares. The threshold is inclusive, so a holding of exactly 10% is reported.

Is the 10% Test on Overall Ownership or Per Class?

Per class. A shareholder holding 9% of the common shares but 40% of the preferred shares is reported on the strength of the preferred class.

Does a Nil Return Still File Schedule 50?

Yes, in full. A corporation with no activity still has shareholders, and who they are has not changed because the corporation did nothing.

It is reported with its business number rather than a social insurance number. A holding structure is therefore visible across the two returns.

Does a Shareholder Loan Go on Schedule 50?

No. A balance owed to or by a shareholder is a balance sheet item reported on Schedule 100 through the GIFI. Schedule 50 reports who the shareholders are.

No. It is filed with the Canada Revenue Agency and covered by the confidentiality rules for a corporation's tax information. A registry's public ownership record, where one exists, is separate and holds different information.

Which Corporations This Covers

This guide is about a corporation incorporated in Canada whose shares are held by people or entities outside Canada. It is a Canadian corporation with non-resident owners.

That is a different thing from a corporation incorporated abroad, and the distinction decides which rules apply.

CorporationWhat it is here
Incorporated in Canada, Canadian ownersAn ordinary resident corporation
Incorporated in Canada, owners abroadResident, and the subject of this guide
Incorporated abroad, managed from CanadaResidence is a question of fact and is not decided here
Incorporated abroad, no Canadian presenceOutside what this site files

Only the second row is straightforward, and it is the common case: a Canadian corporation set up by someone who has since left, or who never lived here.

Corporate Residence and Where It Is Decided

A corporation incorporated in Canada is a resident of Canada. Where a corporation was incorporated elsewhere, residence turns on where it is centrally managed and controlled, which is a question of fact.

Residence is the corporation's own, not its shareholders'. Owners living abroad do not make a Canadian corporation non-resident.

This site files for corporations incorporated in Canada. Where residence is genuinely in question, that is a determination for Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca rather than a form on this one.

The Filing Obligation

A Canadian corporation with non-resident owners files a T2 for every tax year, six months after each year-end, until it is dissolved. Having no activity does not change that and neither does having no Canadian resident involved in it.

The return is the same return. The owners' location changes who signs and how, not what is filed.

See whether a corporation with no activity files.

The Penalty Built on Days, Not Tax Owing

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. The unfiled year still stays open forever, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, blocks a clearance certificate and dissolution, and costs a non-resident-owned corporation $25.00 per day up to $2,500.00.

The last clause of that block is this guide's subject. A non-resident-owned corporation that fails to file faces a charge of $25.00 per day, to a maximum of $2,500.00, and it is built on days rather than on tax owing.

Days lateCharge at $25.00 a day
10 days$250.00
30 days$750.00
60 days$1,500.00
100 days$2,500.00, the maximum
A year or more$2,500.00, the maximum

The maximum is reached in a little over three months. After that the charge stops growing while everything else about the open year continues.

Nil T2 Filing, $300.00 plus HST per tax year

One price for every year and every province. CPA reviewed and transmitted electronically.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Why a Nil Year Carries the Full Exposure

A percentage of $0.00 is $0.00. Twenty-five dollars a day for a hundred days is $2,500.00 whether the corporation earned millions or nothing at all.

This is the one charge in this family of rules that reaches its maximum on a completely empty year. A dormant Canadian corporation owned from abroad is the single most exposed thing this site files for, and the exposure comes from the calendar rather than from anything it did.

Filing the year is what stops the days counting. See filing a nil T2 late.

Other Returns That May Be Due

A corporation with non-resident connections can owe information returns beyond the T2. They are separate filings with their own deadlines and their own charges for lateness.

ReturnConcerns
T106Transactions with non-arm's length non-residents
T1134Interests in foreign affiliates
T1135Specified foreign property above the threshold
NR4Amounts paid or credited to non-residents

None of these is covered by the fee on this page and none is a nil T2. A corporation that may owe one is handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

A genuinely dormant corporation with no transactions and no foreign holdings generally owes none of them, but that is a conclusion to reach deliberately rather than to assume.

Treaty-Based Returns

Where a tax treaty affects a corporation's Canadian tax position, the return may need to disclose the treaty relied on. That is a trading-return matter: a corporation with no income has no treaty position to take.

A nil year reports $0.00 of income from every source, so there is nothing for a treaty to exempt or reduce.

Where a treaty position is in play, the return is not nil and is not filed here.

Signing From Outside Canada

Form T183CORP is signed by an authorized signing officer of the corporation. The officer's location is irrelevant: a director abroad signs the same form in the same way.

It is signed here on a single-use access-controlled screen, with the date and the time recorded on the server in Eastern Time. It is never backdated. Time zones do not change the recorded moment.

The signing rules are in the guide to Form T183CORP signing and transmission.

Getting a Business Number Without a Canadian Address

A business number is needed before a return can be transmitted. A corporation obtains one whether or not its directors live in Canada.

The registered office address on the registry record is the corporation's own, and keeping it current matters more here than anywhere, because correspondence has further to travel and the directors are not nearby to collect it.

See whether a business number is needed to file.

Catching Up Several Non-Resident Years

Each outstanding year is its own return for its own tax year, prepared oldest first. Six unfiled years are six returns, each at $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

The daily charge is per return rather than per corporation, which is why several open years are worth dealing with together rather than one at a time.

See filing five years at once and the guide to catching up on unfiled corporate tax returns.

Dissolving a Non-Resident-Owned Corporation

The sequence is the same as for any other corporation: every outstanding year filed, a clearance certificate, articles of dissolution, then the final T2 running to the dissolution date.

Non-resident ownership gives it more urgency rather than a different shape. Each year the corporation is left standing is another year able to attract the daily charge.

A holding corporation with investment income, a rental corporation and a corporation that paid or received a dividend are not nil. Those are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a Canadian Corporation With Owners Abroad Still File a T2?

Yes, for every tax year, six months after each year-end, until it is formally dissolved. Owners living abroad do not change the obligation.

What Is the $25.00 a Day Charge?

A non-resident-owned corporation that fails to file faces $25.00 per day to a maximum of $2,500.00. It is built on days rather than on tax owing, so the maximum is reached in a little over three months.

Does It Apply to a Year With No Activity?

Yes, in full. It is calculated on days, so an entirely empty year reaches the same $2,500.00 maximum a trading year would.

Does Owning a Canadian Corporation From Abroad Make It Non-Resident?

No. A corporation incorporated in Canada is a resident of Canada. Residence is the corporation's own, not its shareholders'.

Can Form T183CORP Be Signed From Outside Canada?

Yes. An authorized signing officer signs it wherever they are, on a single-use access-controlled screen, with the date and time recorded on the server in Eastern Time.

Are the T106, T1134 and T1135 Covered by the Fee?

No. Those are separate information returns with their own deadlines, and a corporation that may owe one is handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.
